children: “A hair in the flour”
“面粉里的一根头发”
[Voice and freedom]
［声音与自由］

How does one speak out against injustice and the destruction of life on earth? Words and concepts betray us. The concept of freedom is much abused, and yet the idea of freedom is still as important a tool as any for the disenfranchised. Movements split and change. What seems at first empowerment can come to seem an oppressive discipline or an empty rhetoric. To pick among the causes presented to us—as well as those hidden from our view—is a constant work of passion and judgment. It changes who we are. We imagine that we find our “voice” for that moment when a way we have learned to speak seems to fit a critical purpose. We tap into a legacy of speaking to articulate our situation within a general complaint.

人如何发声反对不义与对地球生命的毁灭？词语和概念背叛我们。自由的概念遭到严重滥用，然而自由的观念对被剥夺权利的人来说，仍是重要性不亚于任何其他工具的工具。运动分裂并改变。起初看似赋权的东西，后来可能显得像压迫性的纪律或空洞的修辞。在呈现给我们的各种事业——以及那些藏在我们视野之外的事业——中作出选择，是激情与判断的持续工作。它改变我们是谁。我们想象，当某种我们学会的说话方式似乎适合某个批判目的时，我们在那一刻找到了自己的“声音”。我们接入一份言说的遗产，把自己的处境表达为一种更普遍的抗议的一部分。

The New Order regime in Indonesia came to power in 1966 by silencing one kind of voice and promoting another. The nationalist populism that had been increasingly identified with the Indonesian Communist Party was shattered in gunfire and buried in prison camps. The new state encouraged instead the voice of modernization and development. Citizens were asked to remake themselves in that modern discipline that promised future prosperity for both individuals and communities. Indeed, the greatest success of the New Order state in the countryside was the fact that so many rural people came to speak in this development voice. Their worst complaints could be solved, it seemed, by more development—that is, the expansion of the state. Most social analysts quickly naturalized this voice as the proper desire of the poor for self-improvement.

印尼的新秩序政权于1966年上台，其方式是让一种声音沉默，并推广另一种声音。此前日益与印尼共产党联系在一起的民族主义民粹主义，在枪火中被粉碎，被埋葬在拘禁营中。新国家转而鼓励现代化与发展的声音。公民被要求以那种现代纪律重塑自己，它承诺个人与社群都将获得未来的繁荣。确实，新秩序国家在乡村的最大成功，是那么多乡下人开始用这种发展声音说话。他们最严重的抱怨似乎可以通过更多发展——也就是国家的扩张——来解决。大多数社会分析者很快把这种声音自然化为穷人要求自我改善的正当愿望。

Yet even at the height of New Order rule, other voices could be heard. The echoes of Indonesia’s anti-colonial struggle continued to reverberate in criticisms of corruption and calls for social justice. Critics of the state aligned themselves with varied transnational coalitions, ranging from Islam to environmentalism. Rhetorics of morality, on the one hand, and rights, on the other, came to fill the silences left by an earlier populism. Those who gravitated toward cosmopolitan, secular freedoms endorsed causes of human rights, the rule of law, and freedom of the press. Transnational political liberalism thus came to play a role in stimulating Indonesian critical voices.
然而即使在新秩序统治的鼎盛时期，也能听到其他声音。印尼反殖民斗争的余响继续在对腐败的批评和伸张社会正义的呼声中回荡。国家的批评者与各种跨国联盟结盟，从伊斯兰教到环保主义。一方面是关于道德的修辞，另一方面是关于权利的修辞，填补了早先民粹主义留下的沉默。那些被世界主义、世俗自由吸引的人，支持人权、法治和新闻自由的事业。跨国政治自由主义因而在激发印尼批判声音中发挥了作用。

Environmental protection and social justice coalesced in this current. In the environmental movement of the 1980s and 1990s, rights discourse—human rights, customary property rights, indigenous cultural rights—addressed the intertwined problems of landscape destruction and authoritarian rule. Yet the relevance of rights to the problems at hand was not self-evident; it had to be established step by step, and often in a confused dance in which even partners stepped on each other’s feet. Terms were translated back and forth from foreign languages and across multiple vernacular uses. Local viewpoints proliferated, and angry debates flourished. As in any movement, it was often difficult to differentiate allies from enemies. Social criticism and political mobilization could only advance through friction.

环境保护与社会正义在这股潮流中汇合。在20世纪80和90年代的环保运动中，权利话语——人权、习惯财产权、原住民文化权利——回应了地景破坏与威权统治相互交织的问题。然而，权利与眼前问题的相关性并非不言自明；它必须一步一步地建立起来，而且往往是在一场混乱的舞蹈中，甚至舞伴也会踩到彼此的脚。术语在外语与本地语言之间来回翻译，并在多种地方性用法中转换。地方观点激增，激烈的辩论蓬勃展开。如同任何运动，往往很难区分盟友与敌人。社会批评和政治动员只能通过摩擦推进。
One place to begin is with some very parochial stories. My own attempts to find a voice frame those of my companions in the Meratus Mountains.
一个起点是一些非常地方性的故事。我自己寻找声音的尝试，为我在梅拉图斯山脉的同伴们的尝试提供了框架。

After many years of political quietude in the countryside, people are talking. In the Meratus Mountains, the talk is of timber companies, which are destroying Meratus forests. I have been spending the summer in a mountainous area not yet in the range of the loggers, but people know that the loggers are moving up the slopes on both sides. When I hike down to the Meratus resettlement village of Niwan, the renowned shaman Awat Kilay, a mentor of mine, pulls me aside. “The logging companies are ruining our land,” he tells me. “When you go to Jakarta, you must tell Ibu Tien to stop.” Ibu Tien is the wife of then-president Suharto, and popularly imagined as the sponsor of much resource exploitation. I protest that I don’t have the status to make an appointment with Ibu Tien. He tries to talk me through it, conjuring an image of a pleasant lunch with the First Lady sipping tea. The task is urgent! I am embarrassed; I don’t know how to explain my weakness and my lack of courage. I tell him that all I know how to do is write. He becomes thoughtful, taking in my explanation. He tells me to write with a critical attitude. “Be a hair in the flour,” he explains. He is speaking of the rice flour used to prepare ritual cakes for the appeasement of authority. Communities offer ceremonial cakes to the spirits to keep them from taxing and troubling their human subjects; so, too, such appeasement is understood as the stuff of obedience to the state. A hair in the flour is a disturbance of everyday subservience and routine. A hair in the flour ruins the legitimacy of power. It is a benediction for my work and an inspiration for what I must continue to learn. I have repeated it to myself throughout the research for this book and its writing.

在乡村多年的政治沉寂之后，人们开始议论。在梅拉图斯山脉，议论的是正在毁坏梅拉图斯森林的木材公司。我整个夏天都在一个尚未进入伐木者范围的山区度过，但人们知道伐木者正从两侧山坡向上推进。当我徒步下到梅拉图斯人的重新安置村尼万时，著名萨满阿瓦特·基莱——我的一位导师——把我拉到一边。“伐木公司正在毁掉我们的土地，”他告诉我。“你去雅加达时，必须告诉蒂恩夫人停下来。”蒂恩夫人是时任总统苏哈托的妻子，在民间想象中是许多资源开发的赞助者。我辩解说，我没有地位去预约会见蒂恩夫人。他试图说服我，想象第一夫人品着茶、共进愉快午餐的画面。任务紧迫！我很尴尬；我不知道如何解释我的软弱和缺乏勇气。我告诉他，我只会写作。他若有所思，接受了我的解释。他叫我带着批判态度去写。“做面粉里的一根头发，”他解释说。他说的是用来制作安抚权威的仪式糕饼的米粉。社群向精灵献上仪式糕饼，以免它们向人类臣民征税和找麻烦；同样，这种安抚也被理解为服从国家的东西。面粉里的一根头发是对日常服从与常规的扰乱。面粉里的一根头发毁掉权力的合法性。这是对我工作的祝福，也是对我必须继续学习之物的启发。在本书的研究和写作过程中，我一直对自己重复这句话。

To write as a hair in the flour is to look for weaknesses, confusions, and gaps in business as usual. Without such friction, why would we bother to try to change anything? As a hair in the flour I tell of utopian social movements even where they are not victorious. These movements keep alive our sense that the forms of hierarchy and coercion we take most for granted can yet be dislodged. If I tell more about mobilizations for environmental protection and social justice than I do of suffocating development initiatives, it is to offer the former the chance to rattle the hegemony of the latter.
作为面粉里的一根头发去写作，就是寻找一切照常运转中的弱点、混乱和空白。没有这样的摩擦，我们为什么要费心去改变什么？作为面粉里的一根头发，我讲述乌托邦社会运动，即使它们并未获胜。这些运动让我们保持一种感觉：我们最视为理所当然的等级与强制形式仍然可以被撼动。如果我更多讲述环境保护与社会正义的动员，而较少讲述令人窒息的发展举措，那是为了给前者一个机会，去撼动后者的霸权。

But let me return to 1986. One evening, when family and friends have gathered, Awat Kilay gives a rousing speech. “The timber companies are colonizers!” he declares. “We fought the colonizers in the revolution, and we can fight them again!” I am struck that he uses the rhetoric of Indonesia’s struggle for independence. The timber company in this area is Indonesian, but that does not blunt its alien status. The trope of liberation seems quite right. It is a magnificent speech. But I doubt that it moves the young men whom he is trying most to impress. The young men are divided among themselves and cautious in assessing the words of Awat Kilay, who has spent many years living with the stigma of arrest and harassment for having attended a Communist-inspired land reform workshop in the 1960s. Awat Kilay’s son, Ma Igul, is handsome and ambitious, but better known for entrepreneurial than political endeavor. His family jokes that he has twice converted to Islam, and twice been circumcised, to improve his connections with Muslim traders. My adopted brother Ma Salam, a nephew of Awat Kilay, aspires to political leadership in his own mountain village of Rajang but holds a grudge against Awat Kilay for an imagined slight in his childhood. The awkward relation between these three alone is enough to divide communal sentiment—and to stop me from romanticizing Meratus Dayaks as a united cultural force. Instead, I must pick through the fragments and consider my possibilities of dialogue with each.

但让我回到1986年。一天晚上，家人朋友聚在一起，阿瓦特·基莱发表了一场振奋人心的演讲。“木材公司是殖民者！”他宣称。“我们在革命中与殖民者战斗过，我们可以再次与他们战斗！”我注意到他使用了印尼争取独立的修辞。这个地区的木材公司是印尼公司，但这并未削弱其外来者地位。解放的比喻似乎相当恰当。这是一场宏大的演讲。但我怀疑它是否打动了他最想打动的那些年轻人。年轻人内部有分歧，而且在评价阿瓦特·基莱的话时很谨慎；他因20世纪60年代参加过一个共产党启发的土地改革工作坊，多年来一直生活在被捕和骚扰的污名中。阿瓦特·基莱的儿子马·伊古尔英俊而有野心，但更为人知的是创业而非政治事业。他的家人开玩笑说，他两次皈依伊斯兰教、两次行割礼，以改善与穆斯林商人的关系。我的结义兄弟马·萨拉姆是阿瓦特·基莱的侄辈，渴望在自己山中的拉让村获得政治领导权，却因童年时想象中的一次怠慢而对阿瓦特·基莱怀恨在心。仅这三人之间别扭的关系，就足以分裂社群情感——也足以阻止我把梅拉图斯达雅克人浪漫化为一股统一的文化力量。相反，我必须梳理碎片，并考虑我与每个人对话的可能性。

Luckily, Meratus mobilization against logging does not depend on this little gathering. It is centered not in Niwan or Rajang, where the loggers have not yet encroached, but in the adjacent village of Manggur. Through a somewhat inadvertent coalescence of activists, nature lovers, and village elders (in this case, a tightly united sibling set), a small victory is achieved, and the logging company is asked to leave village forests in this area alone. (I tell the story in chapter 7.) The logging company is so angry at being asked to leave that they destroy the area around their base camp, dumping gasoline and strewing machinery around the forest. For the next fifteen years, logging companies attack other areas of the Meratus Mountains, but they leave this sector alone. (Niwan, Rajang, and Manggur are on the west side of the Meratus Mountains. The frontier area I describe in chapter 1 is on the east side, where logging proceeds without pause.) Only in the late 1990s does activism from this sector once again take on an important role in giving voice to Meratus aspirations. The small victories and betrayals of this time—in which the earlier history of factions, transcriptions, and voicings of freedom bear fruit—make this a story worth telling to introduce the frictions of liberal politics.

幸运的是，梅拉图斯人反对伐木的动员并不依赖这次小聚会。它的中心不在伐木者尚未侵入的尼万或拉让，而在邻近的芒古尔村。通过活动家、自然爱好者和村中长者（这里是彼此紧密团结的一组兄弟姐妹）某种不经意间的汇聚，取得了一次小胜利，伐木公司被要求不要动这一地区的村有森林。（我在第七章讲述这个故事。）伐木公司对被要求离开如此愤怒，以至于毁坏了他们大本营周围地区，把汽油倒进森林，并将机械散置各处。此后十五年，伐木公司攻击梅拉图斯山脉的其他地区，却未再侵扰这一片地区。（尼万、拉让和芒古尔位于梅拉图斯山脉西侧。我在第一章描述的边疆地区位于东侧，那里伐木不间断地进行。）只有在20世纪90年代末，来自这一片区的活动主义才再次在赋予梅拉图斯人愿望以声音方面发挥重要作用。此时的小胜利与背叛——派系、转录和自由发声的更早历史在其中结出果实——使这个故事值得讲述，用以引入自由派政治的摩擦。

In the 1990s, activism grew in Manggur, Rajang, and Niwan. Village leaders worked back and forth between different kinds of regional sponsors, mixing the rhetoric of development, on the one hand, and conservation, on the other. Community strength might be gathered from development grants, ecotourism, political patronage, property registration, or environmental advocacy: The most ambitious leaders aimed to draw them all to their villages. After the New Order fell in 1998, the national political situation grew lively and confused. With their political sponsors in trouble, resource exploitation companies experienced a time of insecurity, and community options for protest widened. An archipelago-wide alliance of indigenous people gathered together in Jakarta in 1999 to demand redress for the state’s nonrecognition of their rights. Manggur elders were there representing Meratus Dayaks. It was a thrilling moment for the development of new political ambitions and dreams. “If the State does not acknowledge us, we will not acknowledge the State,” the delegates wrote in their report (AMAN 1999: 9). They went on to refuse state claims to their lands and resources, to reject the state’s labels for them, to criticize the use of the armed forces in domestic affairs, to note the importance of women’s equality, and to demand full participation in the political process.

20世纪90年代，活动主义在芒古尔、拉让和尼万发展起来。村中领袖在不同类型的地区支持者之间来回运作，把发展修辞与保护修辞结合起来。社群力量可能从发展拨款、生态旅游、政治庇护、财产登记或环境倡导中汇聚起来：最有野心的领袖想把它们全都带到自己的村庄。1998年新秩序倒台后，国家政治局势变得活跃而混乱。随着政治赞助者陷入困境，资源开发公司经历了一段不安全时期，社群抗议的选择也扩大了。1999年，一个全群岛原住民联盟在雅加达集会，要求纠正国家对其权利的不承认。芒古尔的长者们代表梅拉图斯达雅克人出席了会议。这是发展新政治抱负与梦想的激动时刻。“如果国家不承认我们，我们也不承认国家，”代表们在报告中写道（AMAN 1999: 9）。他们进而拒绝国家对其土地和资源的主张，拒绝国家强加给他们的标签，批评在国内事务中使用武装部队，指出妇女平等的重要性，并要求充分参与政治过程。

In 1999, too, a new logging threat emerged in the central Meratus Mountains. In November, the regional government had announced an exchange of the sort misleadingly made famous as a “win-win” deal by the U.S. Clinton administration. In exchange for the conservation of a piece of logged-out forest near the east coast, the government would offer the heavily forested central Meratus Mountains to the Korea Development Company, known as Kodeco. The government planned a special economic zone on the east coast to complement Kodeco’s already thriving cement and plywood factories there. Planners hoped to use a small piece of Kodeco’s used-up logging concession in the area as a water catchment area for the special economic zone. But before environmental studies could be done on the feasibility of this idea, and while the special economic zone was still a gleam in a planner’s eye, Kodeco was already surveying the Meratus forests they proposed as their exchange (Chamin, Maha Adi, and Hatta 1999).

Activists at multiple levels organized against the plan. Thirty-three regionally based NGOs formed the Meratus Advocacy Alliance (Aliansi Advokasi Meratus) to advocate for the Meratus and their forests. They pointed out that the logging plan required the government to change the classification of a forest that had long been considered a watershed protection area. They reminded the public of great floods that followed previous episodes of logging. They researched biodiversity and surveyed the opinions of Meratus residents of the forest. They contacted national and international news media, asking them to bring the eyes of the world to their campaign (Aliansi Advokasi Meratus 2000).

也是在1999年，中梅拉图斯山脉出现了新的伐木威胁。11月，地区政府宣布了一项交换安排；这类安排被美国克林顿政府冠以误导性的“双赢”之名而广为人知。为换取东海岸附近一片采伐殆尽森林的保护，政府将把森林茂密的中梅拉图斯山脉提供给韩国开发公司，即 Kodeco。政府计划在东海岸建立一个经济特区，以补充 Kodeco 在那里已经兴旺的水泥和胶合板工厂。规划者希望把 Kodeco 在该地区已采伐殆尽的特许采伐区中的一小块地用作经济特区的集水区。但在对该设想可行性进行环境研究之前，在经济特区还只是规划者心中的初步构想时，Kodeco 就已经在勘测他们提议作为交换的梅拉图斯森林（Chamin, Maha Adi, and Hatta 1999）。

多个层面的活动家组织起来反对该计划。33个地区性非政府组织组成梅拉图斯倡导联盟（Aliansi Advokasi Meratus），为梅拉图斯人及其森林倡导。他们指出，伐木计划要求政府改变一片长期被视为水源保护区的森林的分类。他们提醒公众注意以往伐木之后发生的特大洪水。他们研究生物多样性，并调查森林中梅拉图斯居民的意见。他们联系国内外新闻媒体，请他们把世界的目光带向这场运动（Aliansi Advokasi Meratus 2000）。

Meratus village leaders also became active in the campaign. Meetings were convened, bringing participants from many villages into common discussions of the problem. But as the campaign gained steam, Kodeco became active in its own Meratus patronage.

Kodeco representatives identified key Meratus leaders, wowed them on helicopter tours of company operations, and offered them and their communities substantial “community development” funds in exchange for their support for Kodeco’s logging plans. This was money in hand, a real good as opposed to the unlikely success of environmentalist dreams. A number of leaders changed sides, offering their support for Kodeco’s plan for “development.”
梅拉图斯村庄的领袖们也积极投入这场运动。会议召开，把许多村庄的参与者带入对问题的共同讨论。但随着运动势头增强，Kodeco 开始积极在梅拉图斯施行自己的庇护。
Kodeco 代表确定了关键的梅拉图斯领袖，用直升机参观公司作业让他们惊叹，并向他们及其社群提供大笔“社区发展”资金，以换取他们对 Kodeco 伐木计划的支持。这是实实在在到手的钱，与环保梦想渺茫的成功形成对比。一些领袖改变了立场，支持 Kodeco 的“发展”计划。

By March 2000, the political scene was polarized. On March 13, forty anti-logging Meratus leaders gathered at the provincial capital. An NGO ally made the inflammatory statement that was used as a newspaper headline in the Banjarmasin Post (March 14, 2000): “We are ready to burn down Kodeco.” Meanwhile, a Meratus spokesperson offered a more sober explanation of the protest: “We declare that we reject the plan to change the classification of the forest and its nature reserves for Kodeco Timber Company” (ibid.). This was not to be the last word. On March 14, almost one hundred Meratus Dayaks appeared, and this time they were demonstrating for Kodeco. “We are ready to accept any investor who profits from the Meratus Mountains, because we also want to be prosperous,” said a spokesman (Banjarmasin Post, March 15, 2000).

到2000年3月，政治场面极化。3月13日，40位反对伐木的梅拉图斯领袖在省会聚集。一位非政府组织盟友发表了煽动性言论，被《班贾尔马辛邮报》用作新闻标题（2000年3月14日）：“我们准备烧掉 Kodeco。”与此同时，一位梅拉图斯发言人对抗议作了更冷静的解释：“我们宣布，我们拒绝为 Kodeco 木材公司改变森林及其自然保护区分类的计划”（同上）。这还不是最后的话。3月14日，将近100名梅拉图斯达雅克人出现，这一次他们是来为 Kodeco 示威的。“我们准备接受任何从梅拉图斯山脉获利的投资者，因为我们也想繁荣，”一位发言人说（《班贾尔马辛邮报》，2000年3月15日）。

By this time, my old friend Awat Kilay had succumbed to tuberculosis, and the next generation had grown into roles as village leaders. Naturally, Ma Igul and Ma Salam, who never had been friends, were on opposite sides of the controversy. Ma Igul stood for the right to development. He spoke for the prosperity to be ushered in by the timber company, for the benefit of all entrepreneurs. He himself was ready to gather up the forest products from soon-to-be-logged areas to bring in that otherwise wasted wealth. In contrast, Ma Salam was a leader of the opposition, speaking for the rights of villages to manage their own resources. He led mapping exercises to define village territories and spoke to regional officials about the importance of village-based conservation and development. He worked with the Meratus Advocacy Alliance, showing them how to make their work locally relevant. But local factions had taken over the debate.

到这时，我的老朋友阿瓦特·基莱已因肺结核去世，下一代已担起村中领袖的角色。自然，从未做过朋友的马·伊古尔和马·萨拉姆在这场争议中站在对立面。马·伊古尔代表发展的权利。他为木材公司即将带来的繁荣发声，说这将惠及所有企业家。他本人也准备把即将被采伐地区的林产品收集起来，把那些本来会被浪费的财富换成钱。相比之下，马·萨拉姆是反对派领袖，为村庄管理自己资源的权利发声。他领导测绘工作以界定村庄领土，并向地区官员讲述以村庄为基础的保护与发展的重要性。他与梅拉图斯倡导联盟合作，教他们如何让自己的工作在地方上具有相关性。但地方派系已经接管了辩论。

Regional factions were also at play. In 2000, resource licensing was decentralized, and centralized control was replaced with negotiations among district, regency, and provincial officials and the varied blocs that aimed to influence them. Anti-Kodeco Meratus were allied with nongovernment organizations, the west-side tourist industry (which saw the death of regional tourism with the destruction of the forests), and a number of regency-level government representatives from the west side. The pro-Kodeco faction included the newly elected governor and the east-side regency officials who were already deeply involved with Kodeco’s extensive operations. The governor was able to move the decision to the east-side regency, thus putting Kodeco’s bloc in charge. Debate, however, continued. “Environmental minister rejects Meratus switch but provincial government persists in carrying it out,” read one headline in March 2003 (Radar Banjar, March 18, 2003).

地区派系也在起作用。2000年，资源许可权下放，集中控制被区、县和省级官员以及试图影响他们的各种集团之间的谈判取代。反 Kodeco 的梅拉图斯人与非政府组织、西侧旅游业（它看到森林被毁后区域旅游的死亡）以及一些西侧的县级政府代表结盟。亲 Kodeco 派包括新当选的省长，以及已经深度卷入 Kodeco 广泛业务的东侧县官员。省长把决定权转到东侧县，从而让 Kodeco 的集团掌权。然而辩论仍在继续。“环境部长拒绝梅拉图斯交换，但省政府坚持实施，”2003年3月的一条标题写道（Radar Banjar，2003年3月18日）。

Conventions of news reporting would suggest I stop the story there, with the delineation of factions. Yet this would ignore everything else that has happened in the province over the last twenty-five years. During that time, Kodeco has logged most of the east side of the Meratus Mountains, creating the frontier described in chapter 1. The ecological results have been dramatic, ranging from total loss of tree cover, to its replacement with monocrop plantations, to the skimpy residual forests that were so badly burned in the great fires of 1997. One can say unequivocally that the ecological function of the forest has been badly compromised, biodiversity drastically reduced, and erosion on slopes and river silting and flooding have become major problems. (To add insult to injury, Kodeco has designated some clearcut areas “community forests.”) Meanwhile, this destruction has not brought prosperity to the region and its inhabitants. Profits have been shipped out of the region. The luxury of Kodeco’s compound has not been reproduced in villages. Meratus residents have been politically and economically marginalized by the flood of migrants who have followed the frontier economy. Forest-based livelihoods are no longer possible. Where compensation has been offered for forest land and resources, it in no way matches what would be required to make a living. There are now some wrist watches, televisions, and motorcycles, but these are a poor substitute for agro-forestry livelihoods. With them have come hunger, poverty, and depression. To imagine that Kodeco would take more social or environmental responsibility in its logging of the remaining healthy forest—without even being pressed—is wishful thinking.

新闻报导惯例会建议我在划分派系后就此打住。然而这会忽略过去25年该省发生的一切。在此期间，Kodeco 采伐了梅拉图斯山脉东侧的大部分地区，制造了第一章描述的边疆。生态后果十分戏剧性，从树木覆盖完全丧失，到被单一作物种植园取代，再到1997年大火中严重烧毁的稀疏残存森林。可以毫不含糊地说，森林的生态功能遭到严重损害，生物多样性急剧减少，山坡侵蚀、河流淤积和洪水已成为主要问题。（雪上加霜的是，Kodeco 把一些皆伐区指定为“社区森林”。）与此同时，这种破坏并未给该地区及其居民带来繁荣。利润被运出该地区。Kodeco 大院的奢华没有在村庄中重现。梅拉图斯居民因追随边疆经济的移民潮而在政治上和经济上被边缘化。以森林为基础的生计不再可能。即使为林地和资源提供补偿，也远不足以维持生计。现在有一些手表、电视和摩托车，但它们是农林复合生计的糟糕替代品。与它们同来的是饥饿、贫困和抑郁。想象 Kodeco 在采伐剩余健康森林时会承担更多社会或环境责任——甚至无需别人施压——是一厢情愿。

It is with this background information that one can see that the two sides of the struggle have rather different stakes. The pro-Kodeco faction hopes to get some trace of the wealth for themselves before it slips entirely out of the province. The anti-Kodeco faction wants to change the terms of the discussion. Their protests challenge the status quo of corporate privilege, rather than trying to make a small place inside its net. The implications of each are politically different—for the forests, for Meratus communities, and for the wider public in and beyond South Kalimantan. It is a great frustration to me that nothing I can think of to write seems likely in itself to tip the balance.
正是在这种背景下，人们才能看出斗争双方的利害关系相当不同。亲 Kodeco 派希望趁财富完全滑出本省之前为自己分得一点财富。反 Kodeco 派想改变讨论的条件。他们的抗议挑战公司特权的现状，而不是试图在其网中谋得一个小位置。两者各自的影响在政治上是不同的——对森林、对梅拉图斯社群，以及对南加里曼丹内外更广泛的公众。令我非常沮丧的是，我能想到要写的任何东西本身似乎都不太可能改变平衡。

Still, to write as a hair in the flour means to give the mobilization against forest destruction its due, not just to praise it, but to show how it offers a practical model to oppose global business as usual. How do we convince people that life on earth is worth saving? This is a political question as well as an environmental one. It requires a politics of working across difference in which the goal is not to make difference disappear but to make it part of the political program. Furthermore, the task requires the same breadth of global connection as does frontier resource extraction.
尽管如此，作为面粉里的一根头发去写作，意味着给予反对森林破坏的动员应有的重视，不只是赞美它，还要展示它如何提供一种实践范式，去反对全球既有秩序照常运转。我们如何说服人们，地球上的生命值得拯救？这是一个政治问题，也是一个环境问题。它需要一种跨越差异运作的政治，其目标不是让差异消失，而是使它成为政治纲领的一部分。此外，这项任务需要与边疆资源开采同样广度的全球联结。

Thus, ironically, it seems politically as well as intellectually useful to offer a symmetrical analysis of friction in both the resource extraction industry and its opposition. To show contingencies, gaps, and slippages interrupts claims of the easy unity of the market as it also illustrates the creative possibilities of social mobilization. Each requires attention to the awkwardness of translation and the need to build heterogeneous audiences.
因此，讽刺的是，对资源开采业及其反对者双方的摩擦作对称分析，在政治上和智识上似乎都有用。展示偶然性、空白和滑移，打断了市场轻易统一的宣称，也说明了社会动员的创造性可能。两者都需要关注翻译的别扭，以及建构异质受众的需要。

Politics on both sides of the Kodeco debate involved rounding up local allies by deploying a full array of transnational resources. Kodeco was only offered the central Meratus Mountains as a concession because when informed of the plan to use a piece of its land as a water catchment area, it threatened to sue at the World Court (Chamin et al. 1999). Those who wanted to preserve the forest also spoke of the international context, for example, in attracting tourists, as one spokesperson argued, “from Holland, Australia, Canada, and the United States” (Dinamika Berita 1999). Yet the relation between transnationalism and regional mobilization differed on each side. The pro-Kodeco faction needed to cover up their transnationalism to make participants imagine a local populism. Their transnationalism is a reminder of the alienation of profits and of control by distant elites. It must be downplayed in the making of a locally inclusive “we” who can be imagined as sharing the wealth. This is a sleight of hand, a mystification in which local and global inequalities are covered up. In contrast, the anti-Kodeco faction has the advantages of a more ready-to-hand localism: Their goal is to preserve Meratus rights and forests. Yet they must conjure a transnational “we” to amplify this small cause with enough volume to speak. Translation across difference is key to both ways of achieving political voice—but with contrasting power dynamics.

Kodeco 辩论双方的政治，都涉及通过部署全套跨国资源来聚拢地方盟友。Kodeco 之所以获得中梅拉图斯山脉作为特许采伐区，是因为当被告知计划用其一块土地作集水区时，它威胁要在国际法院起诉（Chamin et al. 1999）。那些想保护森林的人也谈到国际背景，例如在吸引游客方面，正如一位发言人所说，“来自荷兰、澳大利亚、加拿大和美国”（Dinamika Berita 1999）。然而，跨国主义与地区动员的关系在双方那里有所不同。亲 Kodeco 派需要掩盖其跨国性，让参与者想象一种地方民粹主义。其跨国性提醒人们利润流向外部和远方精英的控制。在制造一个可以想象为共享财富的地方包容性“我们”时，这一点必须被淡化。这是障眼法，一种神秘化，地方与全球的不平等在其中被掩盖。相比之下，反 Kodeco 派拥有更为现成可用的地方主义优势：他们的目标是保护梅拉图斯人的权利和森林。然而他们必须召唤一个跨国“我们”，把这一小事业放大到足以发声的音量。跨越差异的翻译是两种获得政治声音的方式的关键——但权力动态截然不同。

The Meratus Advocacy Alliance used translation to evoke a transnationally inclusive public who might jointly cherish the Meratus forest. For example, they argued that “the existence and holistic function of the Meratus Mountains conservation area, including biodiversity conservation, is very much tied to the life and death of many people (
public interest
) and the responsibility of the current generation to the next generation (
intergenerational accountability

)” (Aliansi Advokasi Meratus 2000: 5). The original statement is in Indonesian except for the words I have put in italics, which are in English. Indonesian is fully adequate to discuss public interest and intergenerational accountability. Translation, however, serves a political purpose, building an expansive public in the space between English and Indonesian. “Public interest” emerges in that space; the future to which generations look forward is simultaneously local, national, and global.
梅拉图斯倡导联盟利用翻译，唤起一个可能共同珍视梅拉图斯森林的跨国包容性公众。例如，他们论证说：“梅拉图斯山脉保护区的存在与整体功能，包括生物多样性保护，与许多人的生死（
public interest
）以及当代人对下一代的责任（
intergenerational accountability
）密切相关”（Aliansi Advokasi Meratus 2000: 5）。原文陈述为印尼语，只有我用斜体标出的词为英语。印尼语完全足以讨论公共利益和代际责任。然而，翻译服务于一个政治目的，在英语与印尼语之间的空间里建构一个扩张性的公众。“公共利益”在那个空间中浮现；各代人展望的未来同时是地方的、国家的和全球的。

In contrast, consider the governor’s words of encouragement to the proKodeco Meratus demonstrators. The provincial newspaper goes out of its way to point out that he addressed the demonstrators in the Banjar language (Banjarmasin Post, March 15, 2000). Banjar is the language of South Kalimantan’s regional majority. Meratus understand Banjar but have their own linguistic usages. The governor did not use Indonesian, the official language of the nation-state, but Banjar, the language identified with provincial populism. By including Meratus as if they were Banjar, he attempted to articulate populism—through translation. The newspaper’s readers gather that the demonstrators are being treated, respectfully, as the voice of the common people, the populace the government must support.

Meanwhile, the newspaper reports Kodeco’s suspicion that anti-Kodeco sentiments are spread by outside agitators (ibid.). Who's in and who’s out? Where the antiKodeco faction must conjure virtual outsiders, the pro-Kodeco group must cover up its comprador status, while baselessly pointing fingers at the other guys.

相比之下，想想省长对亲 Kodeco 的梅拉图斯示威者的鼓励之词。省报特意指出，他用班贾尔语向示威者讲话（Banjarmasin Post，2000年3月15日）。班贾尔语是南加里曼丹地区多数人的语言。梅拉图斯人懂班贾尔语，但有自己的语言用法。省长没有使用印尼语——民族国家的官方语言——而是使用班贾尔语，一种与省级民粹主义相联系的语言。通过把梅拉图斯人包括进来，仿佛他们是班贾尔人，他试图通过翻译来表述民粹主义。报纸读者领会到，示威者被尊重地当作普通人民的声音，政府必须支持的民众。
与此同时，报纸报导 Kodeco 的怀疑：反 Kodeco 情绪是由外部煽动者散布的（同上）。谁在内，谁在外？反 Kodeco 派必须召唤虚拟的外部人，亲 Kodeco 集团则必须掩盖其买办地位，同时毫无根据地指责对方。

For both sides then, “voice” was built through intercultural practices, including translation. My job is to make these troublesome translations more apparent: to show that the coalitional structure of such engagements is not just a matter of adding allies, but also of remaking ideas, practices, and local, regional, and global histories. Only in this analytically symmetrical treatment can the differences between landscape destruction and the struggle for life shine through.
因此，对双方来说，“声音”都是通过包括翻译在内的跨文化实践建构的。我的工作是让这些麻烦的翻译更加明显：表明此类参与的联盟结构不只是增加盟友，也是重造观念、实践以及地方、区域和全球历史。只有在这种分析上对称的处理中，地景破坏与争取生命的斗争之间的差异才能显现出来。

en: Kodeco was ready in part because it had become the target of many small protests. In December 1998, a group of villagers occupied Kodeco’s golf course, claiming that compensation for their land had not been paid (Banjarmasin Post, December 22, 1998). In March and April 1999, another group occupied Kodeco’s main offices, demanding compensation for one of Kodeco’s coconut plantations (Banjarmasin Post, March 11, 1999 and April 15, 1999). Villagers felt morally empowered because Kodeco had razed a local cemetery for the plantation. Other companies across the region were similarly under attack. It was time for Kodeco to improve its image.
zh: Kodeco 之所以准备好，部分是因为它已成为许多小规模抗议的目标。1998年12月，一群村民占领了 Kodeco 的高尔夫球场，声称他们的土地补偿尚未支付（

children: Banjarmasin Post

zh: ，1998年12月22日）。1999年3月和4月，另一群人占领了 Kodeco 的总部办公室，要求就 Kodeco 一处椰子种植园造成的损失给予补偿（

children: Banjarmasin Post

zh: ，1999年3月11日和1999年4月15日）。村民在道义上感到有力量，因为 Kodeco 为了种植园而夷平了一处当地墓地。该地区其他公司也遭到类似攻击。Kodeco 是时候改善形象了。

en: The governor may or may not have known that Banjar and Meratus languages, while close, are not identical; he also probably did not care, and this lack of attentiveness is one of the key translation practices here. He addressed the Meratus demonstrators as pian sampaian, “all of you [respected ones]” (Banjarmasin Post, March 15, 2000). Banjar language uses pronouns that differentiate listeners in terms of age and status; pian is respectful. Meratus language has no such status-differentiating pronouns. The governor's respect was thus contingent on Meratus willingness to consider themselves Banjar. Certainly, all the Meratus demonstrators understood the Banjar pronoun; they would have understood Indonesian, the national language, equally well. The point was not comprehension but the making of a form of populism that would work for the state, in alliance with the demonstrators.
zh: 省长也许知道、也许不知道班贾尔语和梅拉图斯语虽相近却并不相同；他很可能也不在意，而这种不留意正是这里的关键翻译实践之一。他称呼梅拉图斯示威者为 pian sampaian，“你们所有人〔受尊敬者〕”（

children: Banjarmasin Post

zh: ，2000年3月15日）。班贾尔语使用按年龄和地位区分听者的代词；pian 是敬称。梅拉图斯语没有这种区分地位的代词。因此，省长的尊重取决于梅拉图斯人是否愿意把自己视为班贾尔人。当然，所有梅拉图斯示威者都听懂了班贾尔语的代词；他们同样完全能听懂国语印尼语。问题不在于理解，而在于制造一种能为国家所用、并与示威者结盟的民粹主义。

en: This illusory share-the-wealth inclusiveness also works by appropriating the words of opponents. In supporting the pro-Kodeco demonstrators, the governor spoke the very words Kodeco’s critics used to make their case. “[W]e will use [the natural resources of the Meratus Mountains] with care to the environment and conservation,” he began, continuing with the claim that, of course, the government would never allow any logging to which the populace did not agree and in which it did not participate (Banjarmasin Post, March 15, 2000). Participatory and environmentally friendly logging would be the government's goal. Kodeco would surely agree, and then it would be left to disgruntled environmentalists and Meratus residents to contest the practice of this agreement.
zh: 这种虚幻的“分享财富”包容性，也通过挪用对手的话语来运作。在支持亲 Kodeco 的示威者时，省长说的正是 Kodeco 批评者用来论证其立场的话。“我们将注意环境与保护，利用〔梅拉图斯山脉的自然资源〕，”他开口说道，接着声称政府当然绝不会允许任何民众不同意、也不参与的伐木活动（

children: Banjarmasin Post

zh: ，2000年3月15日）。参与式且环保的伐木将成为政府的目标。Kodeco 想必会同意，然后就轮到心怀不满的环保主义者和梅拉图斯居民来质疑这项协议的实际做法了。
